summary: This document gives advice on filtering IPv4 packets based on the IP options they carry. It also discusses the operational and interoperability effects of dropping packets because of those options.

eli5.summary: Some letters have odd stickers on the envelope. This explains which ones a mail room can safely throw away and what trouble that might cause.

questions: why drop packets with ip options
what is the loose source route option
subtitle: Which IPv4 options routers and firewalls should drop, ignore or let through, and what breaks when they drop them.

tldr.problem: IPv4 packets can carry options, some of which are risky or obsolete, and blanket blocking can break protocols that still use them.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC walks through each known IPv4 option, covering its uses, threats and the impact of blocking it, and gives per-option advice for routers, security gateways and firewalls.
tldr.outcome: Many options are obsolete and should be dropped, a few must not be dropped by default, and the rest need a configuration knob. Dropping all optioned packets without careful thought is not recommended.

today: RFC 7126 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 186) and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Several options it tells devices to drop were formally deprecated by RFC 6814.

sections.title: Why Filter IPv4 Options
sections.content:
Many protocols use IPv4 options to some extent, so dropping packets that carry them can have operational and interoperability effects. This RFC discusses those effects and outlines what an operator might do in typical enterprise or service provider networks. It is partly derived from RFC 6274.

It notes that blocking optioned packets is already a widespread practice, and describes three approaches: allow only expected options with a default deny, deny unneeded options with a default allow, or ignore options in transit and treat packets as un-optioned. Experiments and data tend to support the first or third as more realistic. Not every device can filter per option type, and an operator may prefer a coarser policy.
sections.eli5: Many networks already throw away letters with stickers. This paper explains which stickers are safe to throw away and which ones cause trouble if you do.

sections.title: How IPv4 Options Are Built
sections.content:
As specified in RFC 791, an option has one of two formats. Case 1 is a single option-type byte. Case 2 is an option-type byte, an option-length byte (which counts the type and length bytes plus the data) and the option data. Every option except End of Option List (type 0) and No Operation (type 1) is Case 2.

The option-type byte has three fields: a 1-bit copied flag (whether the option is copied into every fragment), a 2-bit option class (0 control, 2 debugging and measurement, 1 and 3 reserved) and a 5-bit option number. The IANA IP OPTION NUMBERS registry lists the assigned numbers.
sections.eli5: Each sticker starts with a code that says whether to copy it onto every piece of a torn-up letter, what kind of sticker it is, and which sticker it is.

sections.title: Why Options Can Hurt Routers
sections.content:
Historically, routers used a general-purpose CPU for forwarding as well as management, routing and control traffic. In that design, a flood of packets with options can overwhelm the CPU and become a Distributed Denial-of-Service risk.

Since about 1995, a growing number of routers use specialized silicon (FPGA or ASIC) for forwarding, which tends to be more resilient. Depending on the implementation, such routers can ignore options and forward, drop, or process the option and forward. Any packet that needs the CPU can be a risk, so operators are urged to consider a router's option-handling ability when buying. The RFC also asks implementers to offer filtering both per option type and in coarser form, and points to RFC 6192 for protecting the control plane.
sections.eli5: If one tired worker has to inspect every sticker by hand, a pile of stickered letters can bury them. A mail room with a fast machine copes much better.

sections.title: Advice for Specific Options
sections.content:
Section 4 of the RFC treats each option with the same pattern: uses, specification, threats, impact if blocked and advice.

  • End of Option List (0) and No Operation (1): nearly every optioned packet has them, so devices SHOULD NOT drop packets because of them.
  • Loose and Strict Source and Record Route (131, 137) and Record Route (7): these can bypass firewall rules, map topology and, for source routing, enable stealthy connections and bandwidth-exhaustion attacks. Devices SHOULD offer a per-option knob (drop, forward as if the option were absent, or process per RFC 791), defaulting to drop. Blocking breaks ping or traceroute used with these options, which the RFC says is already nearly impossible because of widespread dropping.
  • Internet Timestamp (68): can reveal time, map topology and fingerprint systems or devices by clock skew. Devices SHOULD drop it.
  • Router Alert (148): can exhaust router CPU, but blocking breaks users such as RSVP. It SHOULD be allowed only in controlled environments and ignored by default, with a setting to honor, ignore or drop.
  • Quick-Start (25): experimental. Devices SHOULD ignore it by default and offer a setting to honor, ignore or drop.
sections.eli5: Two stickers are on almost every letter, so keep them. Stickers that pry into the route or the clock should go in the bin. A few special ones should be ignored unless you know you need them.

sections.title: Obsolete, Security Label and Other Options
sections.content:
Options now obsolete and harmless to block should be dropped: Stream Identifier (136), Probe MTU (11), Reply MTU (12), Traceroute (82), VISA (142), Extended Internet Protocol (145), Address Extension (147), Sender Directed Multi-Destination Delivery (149), Dynamic Packet State (151) and Upstream Multicast Pkt. (152). Blocking them causes no operational problem.

The security-label options are different. For the DoD Basic Security (130), DoD Extended Security (133) and Commercial IP Security (134) options, blocking or stripping can cause the receiver to drop the packet or attach a wrong sensitivity label. Devices therefore SHOULD NOT modify, remove or drop on these by default, but MAY be configured to do so where the option is known to be unused, and SHOULD be able to log per-interface counts.

For the four RFC3692-style experiment types (30, 94, 158, 222), devices SHOULD have an ignore-and-forward or drop-and-log knob that defaults to drop and log, with logging limited to avoid overload. Unrecognized options should get a similar knob. The RFC acknowledges that this advice contradicts the requirement in RFC 1122 and RFC 1812 to ignore unrecognized options, and says it reflects current operational reality.
sections.eli5: Old stickers nobody uses can go. Secret-label stickers matter to people who use them, so leave them alone by default. Unknown stickers can be ignored or dropped, depending on what you want.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Dropping packets with options can reduce the security problems options cause. Many of the options listed are deprecated and cost nothing to drop. However, dropping packets that carry options still in use can cause real operational problems, so dropping all IPv4 packets with any options without careful consideration is not recommended.
sections.eli5: Throwing away every letter with a sticker feels safe, but some stickers are important, so think first.

fields.name: Copied
fields.desc: 1 means the option is copied to all fragments; 0 means not copied.

fields.name: Class
fields.desc: 0 control, 2 debugging and measurement; 1 and 3 reserved.

fields.name: Option number
fields.desc: Identifies the syntax of the rest of the option.

items.label: End of Option List
items.desc: SHOULD NOT drop packets because of it.

items.label: No Operation
items.desc: SHOULD NOT drop packets because of it.

items.label: Router Alert
items.desc: Ignore by default; allow only in controlled environments.

items.label: Quick-Start
items.desc: Ignore by default; knob to honor, ignore or drop.

items.label: DoD Basic Security
items.desc: Do not modify or drop by default.

items.label: DoD Extended Security
items.desc: Do not modify or drop by default.

items.label: CIPSO
items.desc: Do not modify or drop by default.
